summary: The note describes youth coding workshops in the local region, focusing on the annual CodeBright program founded by Karla Mendez and James Liu. It covers the program's practical curriculum, its efforts at inclusion, student success stories, and the economic and policy arguments for integrating coding into school curriculums. It also highlights partnerships among schools, businesses and non-profits that sustain the workshops.
one_line: CodeBright and similar youth coding workshops build tech skills and inclusion, prompting economic and school-curriculum arguments for early tech education.
key_facts: The annual CodeBright Youth Coding Workshop kicked off on September 14th, 2023, at the downtown community center, as a month-long weekend program.
CodeBright was started by tech educator Karla Mendez and software engineer James Liu as a voluntary initiative to reduce disparity in tech education among local youth.
CodeBright attracts over 200 students annually, who develop projects ranging from simple websites to intricate automation systems.
Nearly 50% of CodeBright attendees are female.
Donations and sponsorships from local tech firms ensure no interested child is left out due to financial constraints.
Fifteen-year-old participant Sophia Torres said coding taught her to think logically and be more creative, comparing it to learning to write stories that come to life.
The Johansson twins, Alice and Beth, developed an app called 'StudyBuddy' to help high schoolers manage their study schedules; it began as their CodeBright workshop project.
Local economist Dr. Ryan Cho argues that programs like CodeBright are 'investments in our workforce development' and an economic imperative.
Education board member Anita Grossman advocates integrating coding into the core school curriculum to teach children to think computationally and break down complex problems.
Integration in schools could include dedicated coding classes, after-school programs, or weaving computational thinking into existing subjects.
Partnerships among schools, local businesses and non-profits fund workshops and provide resources, mentorship and internship opportunities.
The workshops also build life skills such as resilience, collaboration and communication, and inspire students to pursue STEM careers.
